question: Can projecting SGD updates away from the top Hessian eigenspace accelerate learning along flatter directions, and can an interpolation with sharp-direction updates recover the stability and generalization that pure Bulk-SGD loses?

key_findings.claim: Bulk-SGD often matches or modestly exceeds SGD on the small image tasks when it remains stable, despite discarding the gradient component aligned with the top Hessian eigenspace.
key_findings.evidence: On CIFAR10-5k, the MLP reaches 41.12% at learning rate 0.1, k=1, holdout 500 versus SGD's 40.84%; the CNN reaches 42.43% at learning rate 0.001, k=10, holdout 500 versus 41.98%. Many other configurations underperform, showing sensitivity rather than uniform improvement.

anchors.section: 3.1 Bulk-SGD as a Standalone Optimizer, Tables 1-2

key_findings.claim: The finding that bulk-only updates continue reducing loss and dominant-only updates saturate holds for most tested switch points after the earliest training phase.
key_findings.evidence: MNIST-5k checkpoint experiments show Dom-SGD making brief progress when switched near step 30 and then saturating around step 50, while Bulk-SGD reaches lower final loss than SGD for most switches and is best for early switches at steps 0-30.

key_findings.claim: Removing sharp directions permits faster initial descent at larger learning rates but drives an unsaturated increase in sharpness and gradient norm that eventually destabilizes training.
key_findings.evidence: Across the reported architectures, activations, cross-entropy and MSE settings, Bulk-SGD's leading Hessian eigenvalues continue growing rather than plateauing. In the 6000-step switch experiment, increasing the bulk learning rate gives an immediate loss acceleration followed by late spikes or divergence.

anchors.section: 3.3 Instability of Bulk-SGD at Larger Learning Rates
4 Toward Accelerated Optimization via the Bulk Subspace

key_findings.claim: Interpolated updates expose a training-generalization trade-off rather than a demonstrated optimizer win: bulk-heavy settings achieve lower training loss, whereas relatively dominant-heavy settings often have higher test accuracy.
key_findings.evidence: The CIFAR10-5k heatmaps vary separate scale factors on dominant and bulk projected gradients. Lower losses cluster with stronger bulk contributions, while the best test-accuracy regions place more relative weight on dominant directions; some extreme combinations diverge.

key_findings.claim: The top Hessian subspace is empirically dominated by generalized Gauss-Newton curvature, while the functional Hessian has much smaller energy and weak alignment with those directions.
key_findings.evidence: For MSE/tanh, cross-entropy/tanh, and MSE/ReLU experiments, the Frobenius energy of the full Hessian and outer-product/GGN term concentrates in the top-k subspace after early training; the functional term contributes negligibly to the plotted dominant-subspace energy.

method.core_idea: Split each stochastic gradient into its projection on the top-k loss-Hessian eigenvectors and its orthogonal complement, ablate the two components, then independently scale them to study acceleration, stability, and generalization.
method.mechanism: Lanczos-style leading-eigenvector estimates define a periodically refreshed dominant projector. Bulk-SGD removes that component; Dom-SGD retains only it; an interpolated update uses distinct inverse scale parameters for the two projections. Hessian chain-rule decomposition diagnoses which curvature term occupies each subspace.
assumptions: The top-k Hessian eigenspace estimated from a held-out subset is sufficiently stable between projection refreshes of 10-100 steps.
The number of classes is a useful default for dominant-subspace dimension.
Small MLP/CNN results on 5,000-example MNIST and CIFAR-10 subsets reflect mechanisms relevant to broader training.
Training-loss Hessian eigenvectors and their projected stochastic gradients are computed accurately enough for causal intervention.

techniques.role: Separates sharp dominant and flat bulk components of every update.
Tests whether each projected update remains effective from different points on an SGD trajectory.
Interpolates continuously between dominant-only, ordinary, and bulk-only descent.
Attributes dominant-subspace curvature to the loss-output versus model-nonlinearity Hessian terms.

evaluations.setting: Three-layer 100-unit MLP and three-layer 32-channel CNN on CIFAR10-5k, batch size 50, 200 epochs; dominant dimension k in {1,5,10,20}, multiple learning rates and Hessian holdout sizes.
evaluations.metric: Final test accuracy and whether loss diverges.
evaluations.result: Stable Bulk-SGD can match or slightly beat SGD, but several larger-k or larger-rate combinations collapse, and no setting dominates uniformly.
evaluations.baseline: Vanilla SGD with matched architecture and nominal learning rate.

evaluations.setting: MLP on MNIST-5k, switching an SGD checkpoint to Dom-SGD or Bulk-SGD at multiple early and later steps.
evaluations.metric: Training-loss trajectory and final training loss.
evaluations.result: Dominant-only progress quickly saturates; bulk-only descent usually continues and early switches reach the lowest loss.
evaluations.baseline: Continuation with SGD from each checkpoint.

evaluations.setting: CIFAR10-5k interpolation grid and MNIST-5k higher-learning-rate Bulk-SGD switch after 6000 SGD steps.
evaluations.metric: Training loss, test accuracy, gradient norm, top Hessian spectrum, and divergence.
evaluations.result: Greater bulk weight accelerates training loss but raises instability; relatively greater dominant weight is associated with higher test accuracy.
evaluations.baseline: Equal component scaling, equivalent to ordinary SGD, plus pure Dom-SGD and pure Bulk-SGD limits.

limitations: All main results use small networks and 5,000-example subsets; there is no modern large-scale benchmark.
Computing and refreshing top Hessian eigenvectors is expensive, and end-to-end wall-clock acceleration is not reported.
The interpolation study is a heatmap, not an adaptive optimizer with a selection rule tested against strong baselines.
The paper offers empirical hypotheses but no convergence or stability theorem for Bulk-SGD.
Generalization claims are based on test accuracy from limited configurations without confidence intervals or multiple-seed summaries in the main text.
failure_modes: Bulk-only updates can increase curvature in directions that were previously outside top-k, causing the projector to chase a moving unstable spectrum.
Increasing k can remove useful descent directions and substantially degrade accuracy.
Noisy or stale eigenvectors can make the projected update neither truly dominant nor truly bulk.
A lower training loss from stronger bulk steps may worsen test accuracy.
Hessian projection overhead can exceed any reduction in optimizer steps.
reusable_insights: Large gradient alignment with a subspace is not evidence that the subspace causes learning; projected-update interventions are needed.
Sharp directions can be dynamically stabilizing even when they carry little useful loss-decreasing signal.
Curvature-aware acceleration should report both optimizer-step savings and the cost of estimating curvature.
Decomposing Hessian energy can distinguish output-loss geometry from nonlinear model curvature before designing a preconditioner.
open_questions: Can a Hessian-free proxy identify bulk directions cheaply enough to yield real wall-clock gains?
What feedback controller should adjust component scales before sharpness explodes?
Do bulk/dominant roles persist in transformers, normalization layers, large datasets, and adaptive optimizers?
Why does dominant weighting correlate with test accuracy, and does that survive reparameterization-aware sharpness measures?

competitive_landscape.title: Gradient Descent Happens in a Tiny Subspace
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational observation that gradients align with a few top loss-Hessian eigenvectors.
competitive_landscape.difference: Gur-Ari et al. infer that optimization may occur in the dominant subspace; the target adopts causal projections and instead emphasizes bulk descent plus a stabilizing dominant component.

competitive_landscape.title: Does SGD really happen in tiny subspaces?
competitive_landscape.relationship: Immediate direct predecessor introducing Dom-SGD/Bulk-SGD and demonstrating suspicious gradient alignment.
competitive_landscape.difference: Song et al. establish that dominant-only updates stall and bulk-only updates retain learning across SGD, edge-of-stability, and SAM regimes; the target adds hyperparameter/switch ablations, instability analysis, interpolation, and Hessian-component diagnostics.

competitive_landscape.title: Suspicious Alignment of SGD: A Fine-Grained Step Size Condition Analysis
competitive_landscape.relationship: Current closest theoretical explanation of dominant alignment and bulk loss reduction.
competitive_landscape.difference: Deng et al. derive step-size regimes in an ill-conditioned high-dimensional quadratic model; the target is empirical on neural networks and proposes component-wise interpolation without a theorem.

competitive_landscape.title: Sassha: Sharpness-aware Adaptive Second-order Optimization with Stable Hessian Approximation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Practical curvature-aware optimizer competitor explicitly targeting stability, flatness, efficiency, and generalization.
competitive_landscape.difference: Sassha uses stable approximate second-order preconditioning and broad benchmarks; the target explicitly projects exact leading Hessian directions on small models to isolate mechanisms and does not yet deliver a compute-efficient optimizer.

competitive_landscape.title: An Investigation into Neural Net Optimization via Hessian Eigenvalue Density
competitive_landscape.relationship: Prior empirical evidence that outlier Hessian directions contain most gradient energy while flat directions contain important remaining loss and path-to-solution components.
competitive_landscape.difference: Ghorbani et al. diagnose full spectral density and optimization hardness; the target turns the sharp/bulk split into direct update interventions and a two-scale gradient family.

novelty_assessment: Reviewer inference after checking the direct dominant/bulk lineage and current theory: the paper's incremental novelty is the systematic Bulk-SGD stability ablation, explicit component interpolation, and empirical link between the dominant eigenspace and GGN rather than functional-Hessian energy. The central discovery that bulk-only updates can learn while dominant-only updates stall belongs to Song et al.; the proposed method remains a diagnostic prototype, not yet a competitive scalable optimizer.
reviewer_notes: Read all 11 extracted pages, including numerical tables and appendix heatmaps. The scaling notation in the PDF uses inverse component parameters; interpretations follow the text's stated limiting cases. Primary competitor records were checked on 2026-08-23.
